title: Requests and Limits
description: Set CPU and memory requests and limits on containers to ensure fair resource scheduling, prevent noisy neighbors, and keep production clusters stable.

data.text: The Resource Problem in Shared Clusters

In a shared Kubernetes cluster, every container competes for CPU and memory on the same nodes. Without resource constraints, a single buggy or greedy container can consume all available memory, causing the Linux OOM killer to terminate other Pods. CPU-heavy containers can starve other workloads of processing time. **Requests and limits** are the solution: they tell Kubernetes how much resources a container needs and how much it can burst to.

terms.definition: The minimum amount of CPU or memory a container is guaranteed to receive.
The maximum amount of CPU or memory a container is allowed to use.
When a container exceeds its CPU limit, Kubernetes throttles its CPU time.
When a container exceeds its memory limit, the Linux kernel kills the process.
Kubernetes classifies Pods as Guaranteed, Burstable, or BestEffort based on resource settings.

data.text: CPU is measured in **CPU units**, where 1 CPU equals one physical or virtual core. You can use fractional values like `0.5` (half a core) or `250m` (250 millicores). CPU is a **compressible** resource — if a container exceeds its limit, Kubernetes throttles it by reducing its CPU time, but the container keeps running.

data.title: Setting CPU requests and limits
data.content: Guarantee 0.25 CPU cores and allow bursting up to 1 full core.
data.code:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: "250m"
    memory: "256Mi"
  limits:
    cpu: "1000m"
    memory: "512Mi"

data.text: Memory is measured in bytes, typically expressed as Mi (mebibytes) or Gi (gibibytes). Unlike CPU, memory is an **incompressible** resource. If a container tries to use more memory than its limit, Kubernetes terminates the container with an OOMKilled status. This is by design — it prevents one runaway container from crashing the entire node.

data.title: Set memory limits carefully
data.text: Setting a memory limit too low causes OOMKilled errors. Setting it too high wastes node capacity. Start with observed peak usage plus a 20% buffer, then refine based on metrics.

Kubernetes automatically assigns a QoS class to each Pod based on its resource settings. This class determines which Pods get evicted first when a node runs out of resources. Understanding QoS helps you protect critical workloads.

rows: CPU and memory requests equal limits for every container
Requests set, limits higher than requests (or only requests set)

data.caption: How resource requests and limits map to Kubernetes QoS classes.
data.definition:

data.title: Set resource quotas for production workloads
data.description: Practice setting CPU and memory requests and limits.
steps: Apply a ResourceQuota to limit total CPU and memory in the namespace.
Deploy an API Pod with CPU request 250m, CPU limit 1000m, memory request 256Mi, memory limit 512Mi.
Deploy a second Pod without any resource settings.
Describe both Pods and note their QoS classes.
Simulate memory pressure by deploying a stress Pod and observe eviction behavior.
data.expectedOutcome: You understand how requests and limits affect scheduling, QoS class, and eviction behavior.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: CPU requests guarantee minimum CPU; limits cap maximum CPU (throttling beyond limit).
Memory requests guarantee minimum memory; limits cap maximum memory (OOMKilled beyond limit).
QoS classes (Guaranteed, Burstable, BestEffort) determine eviction priority.
Set requests based on observed averages and limits based on observed peaks plus buffer.
Use ResourceQuotas to enforce cluster-wide resource constraints per namespace.
data.takeaway: Requests and limits protect your cluster from resource exhaustion and ensure predictable performance for all workloads.
